title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review Standards, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This page consolidates Redwood Inference SRE guidance for defining and operating Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. Intended readers: SREs, Platform Engineers, Product Owners, and on-call engineers.

Goals
- Provide a single source of truth for SLO definitions, ownership, and alerting thresholds.
- Standardize error budget policy and escalations across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
- Describe capacity planning cadence and required inputs for forecasting GPU and networking capacity.
- Capture incident review expectations and postmortem templates to ensure continuous improvement.
- Surface operational tooling recommendations and a canonical runbook template for common failure modes.

1) SLOs & Error Budgets

Introduction
SLOs define acceptable levels of service for our customers and are the primary operational signal we use to prioritize engineering work. Error budgets quantify how much unreliability we can tolerate and drive decisions about feature launches, rollouts, and reliability investments.

Principles
- Focus on user-visible metrics (latency, availability, correctness) rather than internal counters.
- Keep SLOs simple and actionable: one SLO per user-facing capability when possible.
- Assign an owner for each SLO who is responsible for monitoring, alerts, and runbook accuracy.
- Revisit SLOs quarterly or when feature changes affect user experience.

Canonical SLOs (examples)
| Service Area | SLO | Measurement Window | Owner |
| Hosted API - request success | 99.95% successful responses (2xx/3xx) | 30 days | api-serving-team |
| Hosted API - latency | p99 end-to-end response latency < 500ms | 30 days | api-serving-team |
| Embedding pipeline | 99.9% throughput with <10s tail latency | 30 days | embeddings-team |
| Dedicated GPU pool availability | 99.9% scheduled-available capacity | 30 days | dedicated-ops |

How we calculate availability & latency
- Success rate = (number of requests returning expected status and schema) / (total requests) sampled at the edge (load balancer).
- Latency measurements use end-to-end wall-clock from request ingress to final token emitted for text generation; p95/p99 windows are based on the measurement window above.

Error budget policy
- Error budget = 1 - SLO over the measurement window. Example: 99.95% SLO -> error budget 0.05% of requests per 30 days.
- Burn windows: compute rolling burn over 1h, 24h, 7d, and 30d.
- Escalation thresholds (example):
  1. Advisory: burn > 25% of budget in 7d -> product & SRE notified, schedule targeted investigation.
  2. Action: burn > 50% of budget in 7d OR > 25% in 24h -> pause risky rollouts and allocate engineering resources.
  3. Critical: burn > 90% in 7d OR > 50% in 24h -> activate incident response, temporary rollback, notify leadership and customers as appropriate.

Rollout discipline driven by error budget
- If error budget > action threshold: safe to proceed with canary/gradual rollouts per normal cadence.
- If error budget in action/critical: freeze launches that risk reliability (non-critical security patches exempted), increase monitoring, and schedule reliability sprints.

2) Capacity planning

Cadence and inputs
- Quarterly capacity planning cycle + monthly health check.
- Required inputs: current utilization (GPU, CPU, memory, network), forecasting signals (product roadmaps, expected feature launches, customer bookings for Dedicated), historical traffic growth (last 90/180/365d), model changes (new model sizes, quantization changes), and tail-latency/kv-cache hit rates.

Headroom policy and targets
- Production clusters should maintain 20% headroom on reserved capacity for Hosted to absorb traffic spikes; Dedicated pools follow contractual commitments and are sized per customer SLAs with 10% buffer unless contract specifies otherwise.
- Maintain a 14-day procurement/scale lead for GPU-backed capacity for cloud or bare-metal procurement (timeline varies by provider).

Forecasting procedure (high level)
1. Collect utilization metrics and request growth trends from observability dashboards (see Operational Tooling section).
2. Overlay product roadmap and expected model releases.
3. Translate forecast into required GPU-hours and network bandwidth per region.
4. Convert required GPU-hours into requested capacity (instance types / node count) and submit to infra procurement with recommended timeline.
5. Communicate recommended capacity plan to product and finance 3 weeks before runway adjustments.

Scaling runbooks (short)
- Autoscaling trigger: sustained node CPU/GPU utilization > 75% for 15m and request queue depth > configured threshold.
- Manual scale: oncall may request scale up if traffic surge or degraded latency persists after autoscaling checks. Follow the runbook: 1) validate metrics, 2) increase pool by +25% min(1 node), 3) monitor for 15m, 4) if no improvement, escalate to platform team.

3) Reliability initiatives (RIs) and prioritization

Program structure
- Each quarter, SRE maintains a 90-day reliability roadmap with 3-5 high-impact initiatives (examples: KV cache persistence improvements, model warm-start optimization, multi-region failover automation).
- Each RI has: owner, success criteria (quantified improvement to SLO or error budget burn), implementation plan, and rollback plan.

Prioritization framework
- Expected SLO impact (quantified reduction in error budget burn), customer impact (number and tier of customers affected), engineering effort (story points), and operational risk.
- Gate for RI start: expected SLO improvement > 0.5% of monthly error budget or affecting > 10% of customer requests at p99.

Measuring impact
- Use holdout tests and A/B comparisons where feasible. Track metrics pre/post: error budget burn rate, p95/p99 latency, cache hit rate, and cost delta.

4) Incident review standards and postmortems

Incident severity taxonomy (brief)
- Sev 1: Customer-facing outage affecting >10% of requests or any loss of customer data.
- Sev 2: Significant degradation affecting 1-10% of requests or degradation of an important capability.
- Sev 3: Partial degradation with minimal customer impact or internal operational impact only.

Postmortem requirements (for Sev 1/2)
- Must be published within 72 hours of incident detection (initial draft) and finalized within 14 days.
- Postmortem template fields: Incident summary, timeline (timestamped), impact (customers, requests affected), root cause analysis, contributing factors, detection & mitigation timeline, action items with owners and due dates, and lessons learned.
- All postmortems are blameless; focus on system and process improvements.

Incident review cadence
- Weekly incident review meeting to triage and track action items for recent Sev1/2 incidents.
- Quarterly reliability review where frequent postmortems are synthesized into reliability initiatives.

5) Operational tooling and observability

Required dashboards (examples)
- Global SLO dashboard: per-service SLOs, error budget burn, and recent trends (1h/24h/7d/30d).
- Serving health: request rate, success rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec throughput, queue depth, and GPU utilization per cluster.
- Customer-facing: per-tenant latency and error rates for Dedicated / Private deployments (if permitted by confidentiality).

Alerting thresholds (recommendation)
- SLO burn advisory: rolling 7d burn > 25% -> notify SRE + product slack channel.
- Latency alert: p99 > SLO target for 5m and p95 > SLO target for 10m -> page oncall.
- Success rate alert: drop of >0.2% absolute in 5m window or sustained drop >0.05% for 15m -> page oncall.
- Capacity alert: sustained GPU utilization > 85% for 10m or queue depth spike above configured threshold -> page platform oncall.

Tooling recommendations
- Metrics: Prometheus for internal metrics, Cortex/Thanos for long-term storage.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry -> Jaeger/Tempo for request traces and cross-service root cause analysis.
- Logging: structured request-id-correlated logs shipped to Elastic or Loki for debugging.
- Alerting: PagerDuty for paging; integrate with Slack for advisory notifications.

Automation and playbooks
- Automate common mitigations: automatic rollback for canary failure, circuit-breaker toggles, and dynamic throttling of non-critical features under heavy load.
- Maintain a repository of runbooks in Confluence with Git-backed versioning for changes.

6) SRE runbooks (canonical template and examples)

Runbook template (confluence-friendly)
- Title: short descriptive.
- Owner: primary oncall/team.
- Symptoms: observable signals that indicate the problem.
- Impact: what user-facing effects are expected.
- Runbook steps: numbered, conservative first (safe diagnostics), then corrective actions (safe to aggressive).
- Rollback / mitigation: steps to reduce blast radius.
- Verification: metrics to watch after action.
- Post-incident: required notifications and postmortem owner.

Example runbook: "High p99 latency for Hosted Text Generation"
- Owner: api-serving-team (primary), platform-team (secondary)
- Symptoms:
  1. p99 end-to-end latency > 500ms for > 5 minutes
  2. Token throughput drops or request queue depth increases
  3. GPU utilization low but CPU high on frontends (indicates queuing upstream)

- Immediate actions (0-10 minutes):
  1. Acknowledge page and set incident context in Incident Channel.
  2. Check Global SLO dashboard and request-rate spike graph.
  3. Identify whether spike is user traffic (per-tenant) or system (background jobs) by inspecting per-tenant metrics.
  4. If per-tenant: contact customer success for known scheduled jobs; consider temporary rate-limiting for that tenant.

- Diagnostic steps (10-30 minutes):
  1. Inspect trace sample for p99 requests (OpenTelemetry) to find slow service boundary.
  2. Check KV cache hit rate; if hit rate dropped > 10% then prime cache or scale cache layer.
  3. If backend GPU utilization is saturated: follow capacity runbook (scale up GPU pool).
  4. If frontends are queuing: add frontend instances or increase request worker pool.

- Mitigation steps (30-120 minutes):
  1. If canary deploy in last 2h: roll back canary.
  2. Throttle non-essential background jobs via feature flags.
  3. Engage platform team to increase capacity or apply emergency autoscaling override.

- Verification:
  - Confirm p99 latency trending back below SLO within 30 minutes of mitigation.
  - Validate error budget burn rate is declining in 1h window.

- Post-incident:
  - Draft postmortem and publish initial draft within 72h.
  - Schedule a follow-up action review and track action items to closure.

Required runbook hygiene
- Owners must review runbooks quarterly or after they are used in an incident.
- Add runbook execution annotations to the incident timeline (who ran which step and results).

Appendix: Quick reference tables

SLO summary (copy into dashboards)
| name | slo | window | owner |
| api-success | 99.95% | 30d | api-serving-team |
| api-p99 | p99 < 500ms | 30d | api-serving-team |
| embeddings-throughput | 99.9% | 30d | embeddings-team |

Alert thresholds (summary)
| alert | trigger | page? |
| slo-burn-advisory | 7d burn > 25% | no (slack) |
| slo-burn-action | 7d burn > 50% OR 24h burn > 25% | yes |
| latency-p99 | p99 > target for 5m | yes |
| success-rate-drop | absolute drop >0.2% in 5m | yes |

Owners and escalation contacts
- api-serving-team: oncall rotation (primary@redwood.example.com) - page via PagerDuty.
- platform-team: capacity and scaling (platform-oncall@redwood.example.com).
- embeddings-team: (embeddings-oncall@redwood.example.com).

Maintenance and review schedule
- Quarterly: SLO review and capacity planning report.
- After every Sev1/2: postmortem within 72h and action-item tracking.
- Monthly: runbook and dashboard sanity check.
